# Disciplined close-order infantry (phalanx, legion) (`close_order_infantry`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by bloomery_iron, standing_army_logistics
- Core idea: Men who keep rank and act on command beat a larger number of brave individuals, because each man is covered by his neighbours and the formation can be moved, relieved and rallied. This needs constant drill, a clear chain of small units with their own officers and standards (the Roman century and cohort), and a reserve line that is held back. In many accounts of ancient battles, the heaviest losses occurred after one side broke and ran, so cohesion matters more than weapons.
- Pitfalls:
  - Believing better weapons decide battles; drill, cohesion and reserves decided most of them
  - A deep rigid phalanx is strong in front on level ground but helpless on broken ground or when taken in the flank
  - Expecting film-style duels; men in formation push, fence and rest, and the rout does the killing
  - Drill without pay, food and reliable officers does not last
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2450 BC – Stele of the Vultures (Lagash) shows a shielded spear formation; greece: 7th c. BC – hoplite phalanx; c. 350 BC – Macedonian pike (sarissa) phalanx under Philip II; rome: 4th–3rd c. BC – manipular legion in three lines; c. 100 BC – cohort legion, the army of Caesar in 50 BC; china: 5th–3rd c. BC – Warring States mass infantry armies with crossbows; 210 BC – terracotta army shows Qin formations; africa: c. 1816–1828 – Zulu regiments under Shaka, drilled close-combat formations; europe: 14th–15th c. – Swiss pike squares revive drilled infantry
- Read:
  - Polybius, Histories VI.19–42 and XVIII.28–32
  - Adrian Goldsworthy, The Complete Roman Army (2003)
  - John Keegan, The Face of Battle (1976)
